name: THE COPS AND RABE-ERS BURGER (Topped with Broccoli Rabes)

recipe.history:
Broccoli rabe — known in Italian as rapini — is a flowering brassica vegetable that is only distantly related to broccoli despite its name and superficial resemblance. It is native to the Mediterranean and has been cultivated in southern Italy, particularly in Puglia, Campania, and Calabria, for centuries, where its bitter, slightly nutty flavor profile made it a beloved counterpoint to fatty, rich proteins like sausage and aged cheese. The Romans grew and ate a plant scholars believe was an ancestor of modern rapini, and the ingredient appears in medieval Italian cookery texts with regularity. Broccoli rabe's bitterness — derived from glucosinolates, the same family of compounds that give mustard its heat — is not a flaw to be corrected but a character to be respected. Italian cooks have always understood this, pairing rapini with garlic, olive oil, and red pepper flakes to temper and amplify its bitterness simultaneously.

Broccoli rabe arrived in the United States with waves of Southern Italian immigration in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, settling first into the vegetable markets of New York, Philadelphia, and South Jersey. The Philadelphia Italian pork sandwich — roast pork with sharp provolone and broccoli rabe — is perhaps the highest-profile American application of rapini, and it established the template that burger culture later borrowed: sautéed garlicky broccoli rabe as a topping that cuts through the richness of fatty meat and amplifies umami simultaneously. Gastropubs and Italian-American burger joints embraced it enthusiastically in the 2010s, and the combination of broccoli rabe and sharp provolone on a burger is now something of a Philadelphia tradition.

The first time I made sautéed broccoli rabe I blanched it too briefly and it tasted like pure bitterness — like biting into a strong opinion. My Italian neighbor downstairs knocked on my door an hour later, apparently having smelled the distress through the floorboards, and she walked me through the process correctly: a proper blanch in heavily salted boiling water to temper the bitterness, then a hard sauté in plenty of olive oil with garlic sliced thin and red pepper flakes until the leaves are slightly crispy at the edges and the stems are tender. The transformation is remarkable. What begins as confrontational becomes complex and magnificent. That neighbor taught me more about vegetables in twenty minutes than years of cooking shows had managed.

There is a reason that Italian pork sandwiches — and by extension this burger — depend on broccoli rabe: the bitterness and brightness of the green counterbalances the richness of the meat. But that balance only works if the meat is genuinely rich, genuinely juicy, genuinely alive. A medium-rare patty at 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit has that quality. It has rendered fat still present, still flowing, still providing the counterweight that the broccoli rabe is pushing against. Cook the patty past medium rare and that counterweight disappears, and you are left with bitter greens sitting atop dry meat, and the whole equation collapses. Medium rare is not a preference here. It is structural.
ingredients: 450g broccoli rabe, tough lower stems trimmed
1/4 tsp red pepper flakes (or more to taste)
1 tsp red pepper flakes for finishing
instructions: 1. Make the buns: Combine warm milk, yeast, and sugar in a stand mixer bowl. Let sit 5 minutes until foamy. Add flour, salt, egg, and butter. Knead on medium 8 minutes. Transfer to oiled bowl, cover, rise 1 to 1.5 hours until doubled. Shape into 4 balls, proof on a parchment-lined sheet 45 minutes. Brush with egg wash. Bake at 375°F (190°C) for 16 to 18 minutes until golden. Cool on a rack.

2. Make the roasted garlic aioli: Wrap 4 garlic cloves in foil with a drizzle of olive oil. Roast at 375°F for 30 minutes until completely soft. Squeeze garlic from skins into a bowl. Mash to a paste. Whisk in egg yolks, vinegar, Dijon, and salt. Drizzle in olive oil in a thin stream while whisking constantly until emulsified and thick. Taste and adjust salt. Refrigerate.

3. Prepare the broccoli rabe: Bring a large pot of heavily salted water to a boil. Add broccoli rabe and blanch 2 minutes. Transfer immediately to an ice bath, then drain and squeeze out excess water. Roughly chop into 3-inch pieces.

4. Sauté the broccoli rabe: Heat olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add sliced garlic and red pepper flakes. Cook 60 seconds until garlic is fragrant and just beginning to turn golden. Add blanched broccoli rabe. Sauté, tossing frequently, 4 to 5 minutes until the leaves are slightly crispy at the edges and the stems are tender. Season with salt and lemon juice. Keep warm.

5. Prepare the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions (about 175g each). Form each into a patty 4 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick. Press a thumb dimple in the center. Season generously with salt and pepper just before cooking.

6. Cook the patties: Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Sear patties 3 minutes undisturbed. Flip and place a slice of sharp provolone on each. Cook 2 to 2.5 minutes more until the internal temperature reads 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C). Remove and rest 3 minutes.
7. Toast bun cut sides in the skillet fat over medium heat until golden, about 90 seconds.

8. Assemble: Spread garlic aioli generously on both cut bun surfaces. Set the rested patty with melted provolone on the bottom bun. Pile a generous mound of garlicky broccoli rabe on top of the patty — do not be shy with the quantity. Finish with a pinch of red pepper flakes and flaky sea salt. Cap with the top bun and serve immediately.
